### Prerequisites

In this class we take a tour of some of the first counting tools created by humanity. Before starting, we suggest the first two chapters of the *First Steps* section as the initial texts: **Chapter 1: The journey into numbers** and **Chapter 2: To be or not to be...** (<htcite0>).

### Introduction

Humanity spread across the world over almost 2 million years. If we consider only our own species, *Homo sapiens*, this expansion is much shorter: less than 300,000 years (<htcite0>).
Chart 1: Species related to ours over time.
Along that journey, different peoples created their own ways of counting. In this class we take a tour of some of these first tools and of the regions where they appeared.

Reflection 1: One origin or many?

Do you think mathematical knowledge arose in a single place and then spread, or did it appear independently in different regions?

### The Evolution of Mathematics

Mathematical knowledge developed independently in different places and was only later unified by our species (<htcite0>). In this class we highlight maps and the approximate periods when each numerical system appeared, according to our current understanding.

### In Africa: Counting with Bones

The first counting system we know of arose in Africa, about 37,000 years ago. It was inspired by our hands and was recorded with marks made on bones (<htcite0>). Scholars such as Francisco A. González Redondo study these marks to understand when counting began.

The game below uses the same idea: observe the number and place the same quantity of marks on the bone.

source.text: González Redondo, Francisco A., et al.

### In America: The Quipus

The second counting system we study did not arise near the first one. The earliest evidence dates from about 5,000 years ago, in Caral, Peru, although researchers still debate how old the quipus are (<htcite0>).

The quipu is read on the vertical cords that hang from the main cord, and each knot represents a count. Add knots until the cord shows the proposed number.

### In America: The Mesoamerican Numbers

Recent research suggests that a numerical system began to develop in Mesoamerica around <htdate0>. This may extend our earlier understanding, which placed its use around <htdate1> (<htcite0>; <htcite1>).

In the Mesoamerican system a dot is worth 1 and a bar is worth 5. Represent the proposed number with dots and bars.

### In Europe: The Calculi

Quipus and early abacuses are not easy to preserve, so it is difficult to know exactly where some tools were first used. For this reason, we start the European part of the tour with the *calculi*, whose use the sources we consulted date to around <htdate0> (<htcite0>; <htcite1>).

On the calculi, each column has a different place value. Markers below the bar are worth 1 and markers above the bar are worth 5. Move the markers to represent the proposed number.

### In Asia (India): The Hindu-Arabic Numerals

We cannot be sure when the Hindu-Arabic numerals first arose. Writing reached India only about 2,300 years ago, though numbers may have existed before that. They appear in the Ashoka inscriptions dated to <htdate0> and <htdate1> (<htcite0>).

In a sequence, each number follows the one before it by a fixed step. Look at the sequence and choose the number that is missing.
Figure 6: Asia on the world map. Map from Mapswire ().

### In America: The Yupana

Returning to America (*Abya Yala*), we know that the Incas — during the 15th and 16th centuries according to the Gregorian calendar — created a tool to do mathematics. There is also evidence that the *yupana* was used together with the *quipus* (<htcite0>; <htcite1>).

On the yupana, each row holds one digit and the seeds are placed over the grid. Use the buttons to represent the proposed number.

### Conclusion

In this class we reviewed different numerical systems and observed that the time when they were created does not follow the path of human occupation of the world.

As a result, we can draw some conclusions:
- We are all human, and knowledge did not arise in one place and then spread around the world.
- The basis of mathematics was always everywhere.
- We can reach the same conclusions by representing numbers in different ways.

In the next classes, we will learn how to work with these numbers.
